design_detail: Retrospective analysis of post-mortem toxicology records: all 1006 Finnish autopsy cases investigated at the Department of Forensic Medicine, University of Helsinki, during 1995-2000 in which a forensic pathologist certified the cause of death as poisoning by alcohol, a single drug, or both. The 615 deaths from alcohol alone are compared with nine groups of deaths from alcohol (at least 0.50 parts per thousand) together with one of nine drugs, on one outcome: the post-mortem blood alcohol concentration (BAC) at death. The reasoning is indirect: if a drug adds to alcohol's lethal effect, death should occur at a lower BAC when that drug is present. A fatal toxicity index (FTI, annual deaths per defined daily doses sold per 1000 inhabitants per day) is also computed for each drug. The nine drugs are amitriptyline, citalopram, diltiazem, doxepin, levomepromazine, promazine, propoxyphene, temazepam and zopiclone; the only benzodiazepine studied as an index drug is temazepam.
can_establish: That among Finnish deaths certified as poisoning by alcohol, a drug or both in 1995-2000, the median post-mortem BAC was lower when certain drugs were also present than in the 615 deaths from alcohol alone, and that within each drug group the half with the higher drug concentration had the lower median BAC; and how many deaths each drug caused per unit of its sales.
cannot_establish: The risk of dying from any combination (no denominator: people who took the same combinations and did not die are not counted, and the design has no person-time); that the drug caused death at a lower BAC rather than the two groups differing in who they were (the alcohol-only group was older and more often male, and the drug groups contain far more suicides); what happens below fatal amounts, to breathing or sedation; or anything about benzodiazepines other than temazepam, since diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, nordazepam and demoxepam appear only as low-concentration background findings allowed inside the groups.

sample.recruitment: Registry/records: autopsy cases toxicologically investigated at one national centre (Department of Forensic Medicine, University of Helsinki) during 1995-2000, selected by the forensic pathologist's certified cause of death. Finland has a high autopsy rate and centralized post-mortem toxicology; a broad drug screen is carried out in about 83% of cases, at the pathologist's request (p. 282).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Cause of death certified as poisoning by alcohol, a single drug or both. The nine drugs are those present in at least 20 fatal poisonings of each type. Mixed groups required BAC of at least 0.50 parts per thousand (lowest included 0.50). Pure alcohol poisonings had to be free of every other analyte in the screens. Caffeine, nicotine and small amounts (at most 0.20) of 2-propanol and acetone were allowed everywhere, and low concentrations (below 1 mg/L) of diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, nordazepam or demoxepam were allowed in the mixed groups. The lowest drug concentration counted was the lower limit of each therapeutic range, except temazepam, for which 0.1 mg/L was chosen because relevant effects can occur below the therapeutic level, especially alongside other agents with similar effects (p. 282).
sample.demographics: Pure alcohol poisonings: mean age 53 (range 23-85), 544 of 615 men (88%). Drug-alcohol poisonings: mean age 46, 70% men (editors' calculation from Table 1: 276 of 391 men, 70.6%; weighted mean age 46.2). By group, mean ages run from 42 (promazine) to 51 (diltiazem) and the proportion of men from 56% (doxepin) to 84% (promazine) (Table 1, p. 283).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (records). Cases without a broad drug screen (about 17%) could not enter the study; how many certified poisonings that excluded is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Deaths only, and only deaths a pathologist certified as poisoning: the study cannot see anyone who took the same combination and lived, so nothing here is a risk. The groups are not comparable populations: the alcohol-only group is about seven years older (53 against 46) and far more often male, and the manner of death differs sharply (editors' calculation from Table 1: 99.8% of alcohol-only deaths were accidental and none was a suicide, against 141 of 391 (36%) suicides among the drug-alcohol deaths, 63% in the propoxyphene group). Which drugs appear at all is set by what was prescribed and used in Finland in those years; promazine, the most striking result, is described as predominantly prescribed in Finland to people with alcohol problems to relieve withdrawal symptoms (p. 286), so the people in that group are a selected group with heavy alcohol use.

exposure.measurement: Post-mortem toxicology at an accredited laboratory (Finnish Centre of Metrology and Accreditation, 1997): femoral-vein blood collected at autopsy into 1% sodium fluoride, kept at 4 C; quantitative alcohol determination on every sample; a broad drug screen in about 83% of cases. Limits of quantitation: 0.20 parts per thousand for ethanol, 0.02 mg/L for temazepam, 0.1 mg/L for the other eight drugs. Uncertainty of quantitation: 3% for ethanol above 0.50, 41% for zopiclone, 10-20% for the other drugs above 0.1 mg/L (p. 282).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not known: only post-mortem blood concentrations, never amounts taken, timing or route. Median drug concentrations (mg/L) and the therapeutic ranges the paper quotes: temazepam 0.8 (0.4-0.9), citalopram 0.4 (0.01-0.4), diltiazem 0.6 (0.05-0.3), levomepromazine 0.45 (0.05-0.14), amitriptyline 1.0 (0.04-0.2), zopiclone 0.2 (0.01-0.1), promazine 6.2 (0.1-0.4), propoxyphene 5.4 (0.1-0.75), doxepin 3.3 (0.03-0.15) (Table 2, p. 283).
exposure.polysubstance: Handled by design and incompletely. A case entered a group only if alcohol and that one drug were the certified cause, but low concentrations (below 1 mg/L) of diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, nordazepam or demoxepam were allowed, and such benzodiazepines were present in 24-47% of the mixed poisonings by group (Table 2, p. 283; editors' calculation from the group sizes and percentages: about 136 of the 391 mixed deaths, 35%, and 13% of all 1006). The abstract states that low concentrations of some common benzodiazepines were present in 53% of the 1006 cases, a figure the tables do not support (see reporting issues). The paper states that the presence of these low benzodiazepine concentrations did not affect the median BACs of the poisoning groups (p. 283), without showing that analysis.

comparison.controls: The 615 deaths certified as poisoning by alcohol alone, free of every other analyte in the screens. Each drug-alcohol group is compared with this one group; within each drug group, the half with the higher drug concentration is also compared with the half with the lower (Table 4, p. 285).
comparison.matching: None. No adjustment for age, sex, manner of death or anything else; comparisons are unadjusted pairwise tests (Mann-Whitney for medians, t-test for means).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Tolerance to alcohol and to the drug, regular drinking pattern, whether the drug was prescribed to that person, body weight, liver disease, time between ingestion and death, and the setting of the death. None is measured, and all bear on the BAC at which a person dies.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: The alcohol-only group was required to be free of other analytes, while the drug groups could contain low concentrations of four benzodiazepines; the comparison is therefore not drug-free against one drug.

outcomes.instruments: Post-mortem femoral blood alcohol concentration in mass per mass parts per thousand, by headspace gas chromatography; drug concentrations by the laboratory's screening and quantitation methods. The secondary outcome is the FTI: annual deaths caused by the drug divided by the amount sold as defined daily doses per 1000 inhabitants per day (p. 282).
outcomes.validity_norms: Post-mortem BAC is treated throughout as the BAC at death; post-mortem formation, redistribution and the interval between death and sampling are not discussed. The therapeutic ranges in Table 2 are quoted from four different compilations (references 32-35) and are applied to post-mortem blood. The FTI denominator is national sales, not the number of people taking the drug, so it mixes how dangerous a drug is with how widely and how it is used, which the authors say plainly (abstract and p. 286).
outcomes.operationalization: A combined toxic effect is operationalized as a statistically lower median post-mortem BAC in the drug group than in the alcohol-only group, and as a lower median BAC in the higher-concentration half of each drug group. Neither is a measurement of interaction in a person; both are inferences from where deaths fall.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None reported: nine pairwise comparisons against the alcohol-only group (Table 3), nine high-against-low subgroup comparisons (Table 4) and nine FTIs with intervals (Table 5), with no adjustment mentioned.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable to the measurements (laboratory assays), but the pathologist who chose the certified cause of death, and therefore group membership, knew the toxicology results.

analysis.effect_sizes: Median BAC (parts per thousand) and the printed point estimate of the difference from the alcohol-only group (median 3.3, n=615; quartiles 2.8 and 3.8; range 1.0-6.2), with the Mann-Whitney P (Table 3, p. 284): citalopram 3.1, difference 0.3 (9%), P>0.05; diltiazem 2.8, 0.6 (18%), P=0.006; zopiclone 2.7, 0.6 (18%), P<0.001; temazepam 2.5, 0.8 (24%), P<0.001; levomepromazine 2.6, 0.9 (27%), P<0.001; amitriptyline 1.6, 1.5 (45%), P<0.001; propoxyphene 1.7, 1.6 (48%), P<0.001; doxepin 1.6, 1.6 (48%), P<0.001; promazine 1.3, 1.9 (58%), P<0.001. The 95% confidence intervals appear only in Figure 1 as a plot; editors' measurement of the plotted whiskers against the axis ticks on a 300-dpi rendering gives approximately: citalopram -0.60 to 0.00, diltiazem -1.10 to -0.20, zopiclone -0.90 to -0.30, temazepam -1.00 to -0.60, levomepromazine -1.20 to -0.60, amitriptyline -1.80 to -1.30, doxepin -1.90 to -1.30, propoxyphene -1.80 to -1.40, promazine -2.20 to -1.60. High against low drug concentration within each group (Table 4, p. 285): diltiazem 3.3 against 2.0, difference 1.4, P=0.005; levomepromazine 3.1 against 1.6, 1.3, P<0.001; temazepam 2.9 against 2.1, 0.9, P<0.001; amitriptyline 2.3 against 1.4, 0.8, P=0.005; zopiclone 3.2 against 2.5, 0.7, P>0.05; doxepin 1.9 against 1.2, 0.6, P=0.008; promazine 1.7 against 1.1, 0.6, P=0.025; propoxyphene 1.8 against 1.45, 0.5, P=0.003; citalopram 3.05 against 3.0, 0.2, P>0.5. FTI with 95% CI (Table 5, p. 285): promazine 120.8 (97.7-143.9), levomepromazine 47.3 (37.0-57.7), propoxyphene 32.0 (23.3-40.7), doxepin 20.9 (15.0-26.8), amitriptyline 12.2 (9.3-15.2), citalopram 1.4 (1.1-1.7), diltiazem 1.4 (1.1-1.7), zopiclone 0.9 (0.7-1.2), temazepam 0.9 (0.7-1.1).
analysis.covariates: None. The authors adjust for nothing and present unadjusted pairwise comparisons only.
analysis.preregistration_detail: A retrospective records analysis; no protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The statement that low benzodiazepine concentrations did not affect the group medians (p. 283) is asserted without the numbers. The 53% figure in the abstract is not shown anywhere in the tables. Only one benzodiazepine (temazepam) reaches the 20-case threshold to be an index drug, yet the paper's conclusions are drawn for drug-alcohol combinations in general; the companion paper on benzodiazepines (reference 20) is cited for diazepam and chlordiazepoxide appearing safer than temazepam with alcohol, but those data are not in this paper.
analysis.power: Not reported. Group sizes of 23 to 67 give wide intervals, visible in Figure 1: the diltiazem interval spans 0.9 parts per thousand and the citalopram interval includes zero.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among Finnish poisoning deaths in 1995-2000, people who died with alcohol plus one of these drugs had died at a lower blood alcohol concentration than people who died of alcohol alone: 0.6-0.9 lower for temazepam, zopiclone, levomepromazine and diltiazem, and 1.5-1.9 lower for amitriptyline, propoxyphene, doxepin and promazine, with no detectable difference for citalopram. Within each drug group the half with the higher drug concentration had died at the lower BAC (significant for all but zopiclone and citalopram). The drugs that killed most per unit sold were promazine and levomepromazine, far above the rest; temazepam and zopiclone had the lowest FTIs of the nine.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and discussion read these BAC differences as evidence of a combined toxic effect and of a positive concentration-effect relationship, and conclude that all drug-alcohol combinations are not equally dangerous and that a less dangerous alternative could be chosen at the prescription stage, especially where there are indications of alcohol problems or suicide risk (abstract p. 281; pp. 286). The authors state the main limit themselves: the division reflects not only acute toxicity but also the manners of use of these drugs (p. 286) and that more information is needed to separate behavioural aspects from intrinsic toxicity (p. 286). Gaps: (1) a lower BAC among people who died is not a risk and not a measure of how much a drug adds to alcohol's effect; the same pattern arises if the people who combine a drug with alcohol differ from those who die of alcohol alone, and they plainly do here (about seven years younger, more often women, 36% suicides against none); (2) the concentration-effect reading of Table 4 compares the high and low halves of each group, and in groups where most concentrations exceed the therapeutic range (81-96% in five of the nine groups) the high half are largely intentional overdoses; (3) the promazine result, the paper's headline, comes from 31 deaths among people taking a drug the paper describes as predominantly prescribed in Finland to people with alcohol problems to relieve withdrawal (p. 286); (4) the FTI's denominator is sales, so it cannot separate a dangerous drug from a drug given to people at high risk, as the authors say; (5) the abstract's 53% of these cases had low concentrations of some common benzodiazepines is not supported by the tables (editors' calculation gives about 13% of the 1006).

timeline.event: King reported that alcohol lowers the blood drug concentration at which fatal poisonings occur, with a larger effect for amitriptyline than propoxyphene; this paper reports the opposite ordering, similar effects for the two, and notes King's mean BACs were around 1.4 (p. 285, reference 17).
Stead and Moffat reported the same pattern for barbiturates with alcohol (p. 281, reference 16).

The authors' own companion study of benzodiazepines in fatal poisonings: the presence of temazepam lowered the BAC at which a given proportion of alcohol poisonings occurs, while diazepam, chlordiazepoxide and desmethyldiazepam up to 1 mg/L did not (cited at pp. 282 and 285 as reference 20; not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: The approach (comparing the BAC at which people died with and without a drug) replicates earlier post-mortem work from the 1980s for barbiturates, amitriptyline and propoxyphene, and the authors' own propoxyphene figure (median 1.7) matches their earlier unpublished Finnish analysis and a reported median of 2.2 in 200 forensic cases elsewhere (p. 285). For benzodiazepines the evidence inside this literature is thin: only temazepam was studied here, and the contrast with diazepam and chlordiazepoxide rests on the authors' own 2002 paper, which was not among the files read. No study read for this library counts harm among living people who combine alcohol with a benzodiazepine.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article.
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: All three authors are at the Laboratory of Toxicology, Department of Forensic Medicine, University of Helsinki, the laboratory that produced the toxicology results analysed (p. 281). The same group published the 2002 benzodiazepine analysis this paper builds on. Recorded as context, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A study with a denominator and living people: a cohort or case-crossover analysis linking dispensing records to emergency presentations and deaths, comparing periods of benzodiazepine (or other sedative) availability with and without alcohol, with the amount of alcohol measured rather than inferred from death; and, for the mechanism, controlled laboratory measurement of ventilation and sedation with alcohol and a benzodiazepine alone and together.

domains.note: No adjustment of any kind. The comparison groups differ on the variables most likely to determine the BAC at death: age (53 against 46), sex (88% against 70% men), and above all manner of death (no suicides among the 615 alcohol-only deaths against 141 of 391 in the drug groups, 63% in the propoxyphene group). Tolerance, drinking pattern and body weight are unmeasured. For promazine, the paper describes the drug as predominantly prescribed in Finland to people with alcohol problems to relieve withdrawal (p. 286); the group itself is not described.

Accredited laboratory, femoral blood, stated limits and uncertainties of quantitation; but post-mortem concentrations are treated as concentrations at death, with no discussion of redistribution or post-mortem alcohol formation, and no amount, timing or route is known. Zopiclone's uncertainty is 41%.

Deaths only, and only deaths certified as poisoning, with a broad drug screen performed in about 83% of cases at the pathologist's discretion. There is no denominator of people who took these combinations, so the design cannot yield a risk. Group membership depends on the certifier's choice of cause of death, made with the toxicology in hand.
Whether anyone was found, resuscitated or treated before death is not recorded, and treatment would alter both survival and the measured concentrations.
The roughly 17% of autopsies without a broad drug screen cannot be classified; their number and their certified causes are not reported. No case-level missingness is described.

The outcome is an objective laboratory value, but it is a surrogate for combined toxicity, not a measurement of it; the inference from a lower BAC at death to a pharmacodynamic interaction rests on an assumption the design cannot test.

Nineteen comparisons with no correction and no protocol; confidence intervals for the main comparison are shown only as a figure; the claim that background benzodiazepines did not affect the medians is asserted without data; and the abstract's 53% figure is not supported by the tables.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: ROBINS-E overall can be no milder than the worst domain, and two are very high. The data are complete and well measured for what they are, a national series of certified poisoning deaths with accredited toxicology, and the internal comparisons are consistent (Table 3 and Figure 1, Table 4 and Table 5 point the same way). But the question people ask, how risky is it to mix these drugs with alcohol, cannot be answered by a comparison among the dead: there is no denominator, and the groups differ systematically in age, sex and intent. It may be cited for: the median post-mortem BAC in Finnish alcohol-only poisoning deaths (3.3) and in deaths with each drug, with the printed differences; the ordering of the nine drugs on that measure; the finding that within each drug group the higher drug concentrations went with lower BACs; the FTIs as deaths per unit sold in Finland 1995-2000; and the authors' own point that this ordering reflects how the drugs are used as well as their toxicity. It may not be cited for: the risk of dying from mixing alcohol with a benzodiazepine or any other drug; for a benzodiazepine class statement (only temazepam was studied); for any statement about breathing, sedation or non-fatal harm; or for a causal effect of the combination on the BAC at which people die.

key_findings.finding: In 615 deaths certified as poisoning by alcohol alone, the median post-mortem blood alcohol concentration was 3.3 parts per thousand (quartiles 2.8 and 3.8; range 1.0-6.2).

Deaths with alcohol plus temazepam (n=57) had a median BAC of 2.5, that is 0.8 (24%) lower than the alcohol-only deaths, P<0.001. The 95% confidence interval for the difference is shown only as a plot; editors' measurement of the plotted interval gives about -1.00 to -0.60.
key_findings.note: Temazepam is the only benzodiazepine studied as an index drug; 20 cases of a drug were required and no other benzodiazepine reached that number.

key_findings.finding: The printed differences from the alcohol-only median (Table 3) were 1.5–1.9 for amitriptyline (median BAC 1.6, difference 1.5), propoxyphene (1.7, 1.6), doxepin (1.6, 1.6) and promazine (1.3, 1.9), and 0.6–0.9 for zopiclone (2.7, 0.6), diltiazem (2.8, 0.6), temazepam (2.5, 0.8) and levomepromazine (2.6, 0.9); the Results text gives 1.6–2.0 and 0.6–0.7 for these groups (p. 283; diltiazem not named). Citalopram (3.1, difference 0.3) was the only group without a significant difference (P>0.05); all others had P<0.001 except diltiazem (P=0.006). Note: the printed point estimates are probably Hodges–Lehmann estimates from the Mann–Whitney procedure, which the paper does not state; for amitriptyline and doxepin they differ from 3.3 minus the group median (1.7) by 0.2 and 0.1. [The card's 1.6–2.0 came from the text, not Table 3, where amitriptyline is 1.5.]
key_findings.note: The printed point estimates of difference are Hodges-Lehmann-type estimates, not simple differences of the printed medians: for amitriptyline and doxepin the printed difference (1.5 and 1.6) differs from 3.3 minus the group median (1.7) by 0.1-0.2.

key_findings.finding: Within each drug group, the half with the higher drug concentration had died at a lower median BAC: diltiazem 3.3 against 2.0 (difference 1.4, P=0.005), levomepromazine 3.1 against 1.6 (1.3, P<0.001), temazepam 2.9 against 2.1 (0.9, P<0.001), amitriptyline 2.3 against 1.4 (0.8, P=0.005), doxepin 1.9 against 1.2 (0.6, P=0.008), promazine 1.7 against 1.1 (0.6, P=0.025), propoxyphene 1.8 against 1.45 (0.5, P=0.003); not significant for zopiclone (3.2 against 2.5, P>0.05) and citalopram (3.05 against 3.0, P>0.5).
key_findings.note: The divide was the concentration splitting each group into roughly equal halves (temazepam 0.7 mg/L, 28 against 29 cases), and is included in the low group.

key_findings.finding: Low concentrations (below 1 mg/L) of some common benzodiazepines were present in 24-47% of the mixed poisonings, by group: temazepam group 30%, citalopram 47%, diltiazem 30%, levomepromazine 45%, amitriptyline 46%, zopiclone 24%, promazine 29%, propoxyphene 25%, doxepin 33%. The paper states these did not affect the median BACs of the poisoning groups, without showing that analysis.
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from the group sizes and these percentages: about 136 of the 391 mixed deaths (35%), that is about 13% of the 1006 cases, not the 53% stated in the abstract (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Blood drug concentrations exceeded the quoted therapeutic range in 41-96% of the mixed poisonings by group: temazepam 46%, citalopram 41%, diltiazem 65%, zopiclone 68%, levomepromazine 81%, amitriptyline 86%, promazine 94%, propoxyphene 96%, doxepin 96%. Median concentrations (mg/L): temazepam 0.8 (quoted therapeutic range 0.4-0.9), promazine 6.2 (0.1-0.4), propoxyphene 5.4 (0.1-0.75), doxepin 3.3 (0.03-0.15).
key_findings.note: Only in the temazepam group were cases below the therapeutic range reported (18 of 57); for every other drug the table prints a dash in that column.

key_findings.finding: Fatal toxicity index (annual deaths divided by annual sales in defined daily doses per 1000 inhabitants per day), 1995-2000: promazine 120.8 (95% CI 97.7-143.9), levomepromazine 47.3 (37.0-57.7), propoxyphene 32.0 (23.3-40.7), doxepin 20.9 (15.0-26.8), amitriptyline 12.2 (9.3-15.2), citalopram 1.4 (1.1-1.7), diltiazem 1.4 (1.1-1.7), zopiclone 0.9 (0.7-1.2), temazepam 0.9 (0.7-1.1). Note: The denominator is sales, not the number of people taking the drug or the number of prescriptions; the index mixes a drug's toxicity with who takes it and how. The two hypnotics of the nine, temazepam and zopiclone, have the lowest indices. [Finding confirmed; 'the two sedatives' was wrong, since levomepromazine and promazine, with the highest indices, are also used for sedation.]
key_findings.note: The denominator is sales, not the number of people taking the drug or the number of prescriptions; the index mixes a drug's toxicity with who takes it and how. The two sedatives of the nine, temazepam and zopiclone, have the lowest indices.

key_findings.finding: The groups being compared differ markedly in manner of death: 614 of 615 alcohol-only deaths (99.8%) were accidental and none was recorded as suicide, whereas suicides made up 12-63% of each drug-alcohol group (editors' calculation from Table 1: 141 of the 391 mixed deaths, 36%; propoxyphene 42 of 67, 63%).
key_findings.note: Recorded because the comparison of BACs between these groups is unadjusted.

key_findings.finding: The maximum BAC in the promazine group (3.3) equals the median BAC of the alcohol-only deaths, which the authors call especially remarkable; promazine in Finland is described as predominantly prescribed to people with alcohol problems to relieve withdrawal symptoms.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, promazine row, Maximum column (p. 284); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 286)

key_findings.finding: When the 18 alcohol-temazepam cases with only subtherapeutic temazepam (below 0.4 mg/L) were set aside, the median BAC in the remaining 39 cases was 2.2 (95% CI 2.1-2.5), still below the alcohol-only median of 3.3.
key_findings.note: This is the only confidence interval printed as text rather than plotted.

key_findings.finding: The authors state that the combined effect of alcohol and central nervous system depressants is generally considered additive and usually non-pharmacokinetic, and that in fatal poisonings the pharmacodynamic effects are more important although the mechanisms are not fully elucidated.
key_findings.note: An attributed general statement, not a finding of this study.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that in 53% of the 1006 cases low concentrations of some common benzodiazepines were present. Table 2 gives benzodiazepine-positive shares of 24-47% for the mixed groups only, and the 615 alcohol-only cases were by definition free of them; editors' calculation from the group sizes and percentages gives about 136 cases, 35% of the 391 mixed poisonings and about 13% of all 1006.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's figure cannot be reproduced from the paper and overstates by about four times how often benzodiazepines were found. Any claim must use the group-level percentages in Table 2, not the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints the doxepin group's mean age as 45 with a range of 26-40, so the mean lies outside its own range.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one figure in that row is wrong (probably the upper bound of the range). Ages from Table 1 should not be cited without flagging this; checked on the rendered page, so it is not an extraction error. [Propoxyphene part dropped: a mean of 43 in a range of 28-47 is unusual but possible, and the share of suicides says nothing about age.]

reporting_issues.issue: The printed point estimates of the difference in median BAC do not equal the difference of the printed medians in six groups: printed smaller for amitriptyline (3.3 minus 1.6 = 1.7, printed 1.5), doxepin (1.7, printed 1.6) and promazine (2.0, printed 1.9); printed larger for citalopram (0.2, printed 0.3), diltiazem (0.5, printed 0.6) and levomepromazine (0.7, printed 0.9).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed values are evidently Hodges-Lehmann estimates from the Mann-Whitney test rather than differences of medians, but the paper does not say so; a reader subtracting the medians will get different numbers. Both should be reported together if cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% confidence intervals for the main comparison exist only as a figure; no numeric interval is printed for any of the nine differences, and Table 3 gives only P values.
reporting_issues.consequence: Intervals have to be read off the plot (the editors' measurement against the axis ticks is recorded in analysis.effect_sizes and is approximate to about 0.05). A claim citing precision should say the intervals were read from the figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement that the presence of low concentrations of some common benzodiazepines did not affect the median BACs of the poisoning groups (p. 283) is given without any analysis, number or test, although these benzodiazepines were present in up to 47% of a group and are sedatives of the same class as the index drug temazepam.
reporting_issues.consequence: The key internal check on confounding within the mixed groups cannot be verified, and the temazepam result in particular rests on it.

reporting_issues.issue: Eighteen significance tests are reported (nine comparisons with the alcohol-only deaths, Table 3, and nine high-against-low subgroup comparisons, Table 4), and nine FTIs are given with confidence intervals (Table 5), without any correction for multiplicity; twelve P values are printed only as inequalities (P>0.05 twice and P>0.5 for the non-significant ones, P<0.001 nine times).
reporting_issues.consequence: The borderline results (diltiazem P=0.006; promazine subgroup P=0.025) are less secure than they look, and exact P values are missing wherever an inequality is printed.

reporting_issues.issue: In Table 1, accidental plus suicide leaves 1-11 cases per group unaccounted for (58 of the 391 mixed deaths), presumably of undetermined manner, while the cause-of-death columns sum exactly to each n. The Results text speaks of drug poisonings ruled accidental (57) or undetermined (140), but its 'undetermined' counts for levomepromazine, amitriptyline, propoxyphene and promazine (14, 20, 42 and 18) equal Table 1's suicide counts, and 140 is close to the 141 suicides.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text appears to call suicides 'undetermined'; the deaths of undetermined manner in Table 1 are described nowhere, and the table's percentages do not add to 100.

reporting_issues.issue: The study's one benzodiazepine, temazepam, was included with a lower concentration cut-off (0.1 mg/L) than its therapeutic range would give (0.4 mg/L), on the stated reasoning that effects can occur below the therapeutic level, while every other drug was cut at the bottom of its therapeutic range.
reporting_issues.consequence: The temazepam group therefore includes 18 cases that would have been excluded under the rule applied to the other eight drugs, which lowers the group's median drug concentration; without them the median BAC falls from 2.5 to 2.2 (the authors' own sensitivity analysis), so including them raised the group's median BAC and made the difference from alcohol alone smaller. Both figures should be cited together.

disagreements.reviewer: The printed differences from the alcohol-only median (Table 3) were 1.5–1.9 for amitriptyline (median BAC 1.6, difference 1.5), propoxyphene (1.7, 1.6), doxepin (1.6, 1.6) and promazine (1.3, 1.9), and 0.6–0.9 for zopiclone (2.7, 0.6), diltiazem (2.8, 0.6), temazepam (2.5, 0.8) and levomepromazine (2.6, 0.9); the Results text gives 1.6–2.0 and 0.6–0.7 for these groups (p. 283; diltiazem not named).
